How a 17th-century Yemeni ‘sorcerer’ anticipated the modern playbook of the Houthis

The Houthis are the latest force seeking to dominate Yemen. Before them came Imams, Arab nationalists, Communists, jihadists and political entrepreneurs.

Praveen Swami

16 September, 2026 03:05 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

A Houthi follower looks on, during a pro-Iran demonstration, as the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran continues, in Sanaa, Yemen April 6, 2026. REUTERS/Khaled Abdullah/File Photo

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

T he emerald-green damask canopy, its finial mounted with the kingdom’s silver orb-and-pyramid and swaddled in vermillion silk, shielded the midday sun from the Imam’s splendour. To kettle-drums and oboes, two hundred cavaliers marched through the citadel guarding Mokha, their mounts covered with jewels and black ostrich feathers. Then came Al-Mahdi Muhammad bin Ahmed, chosen by God to prepare the pious for the sounding of Israphil’s trumpet on the Day of Judgment. Each Friday, the elderly Imam dismounted from his white horse to deliver the sermon, light pouring off the jewelled jigha on his turban and waistcoat, bound with a “belt of a monstrous size, set thick with large silver plates.”

For hundreds of years, winds carrying coffee, spices and gold also carried foreign gods past the walls Islam had put up against the world. Travellers to Aden encountered the story of a great well dug from Ujjain to the Seraj mountain by a spirit in the form of a monkey, to rescue a princess from Hind kidnapped by the ten-headed djinn al-Ghazāl Darsīr.

The Banias of Kathiawar, bankers to the Indian Ocean trade, built temples alongside the city’s synagogues and celebrated Diwali. “They are the cleverest arithmeticians in the world,” the French adventurer Jean de la Roque—son of the first coffee-maker of Marseille—wrote after his voyages to Yemen in 1708–1713. “They cheat with a wonderful deal of skill.”

Show Full Article

Last week, as the Ansar Allah insurgents seized Mokha and Perim, the world was reminded that wars along Yemen’s coast never quite ended. Drawn largely from the Zaydi clan federations that sustained the Imamate for almost a millennium, Ansar Allah has given Iran a new means to choke global trade. The Red Sea and Suez shipping routes carry 15% of world trade and just under a tenth of seaborne oil and gas traffic.

The war isn’t just about the power-struggle between Iran and the American-led axis of Israel, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia. Since the Imamate began to implode, Yemen’s leaders have struggled to craft a vision of statehood that its diverse peoples could share. Empires, regional powers and entrepreneurs have sought hegemony instead of accommodation—ensuring perpetual war.

Flying the banners of England, Portugal and Holland, warships appeared off Yemen’s ports in the eighteenth century. European competition helped destroy Mokha’s coffee monopoly, while the Imamate’s authority weakened. Local clans like the Yaf’i looted Mokha. Muhammad al-Shawkani blamed the crisis on the betrayal of shari’a by Imams who put wealth before Islam. His words helped prepare the ground for a rebellion by followers of Ibrahim al-Mahatwari, who believed him a sorcerer and the Mahdi of Shi’a prophecy.

Large numbers of Bāniyāns (Hindus/Jains) and Jews were massacred at Hajjah, ‘Affar and al-Ṣalabah before the Imam’s armies hunted down and executed the sorcerer [ Ṣanʻāʼ: An Arabian Islamic city, edited by RB Serjeant and Ronald Lewcock (1983), page 434 ]. The war was never quite extinguished.

Two nations, many wars The Big Turban , the American doctor Girard Foster called Ahmad bin Yahya Hamidaddin. Excess, bullet injuries and an endocrine disorder had ravaged the Imam’s body, and his mind had been hollowed by heroin. Faced with Arab nationalism, he joined Yemen to the United Arab States with Egypt and Syria. Yemen withdrew from the arrangement in 1961, earning Egypt’s ire, and he married the teenage daughter of a Zaydi chief threatening to pillage Ta’iz. Yahya was in no position to consummate the marriage. Even his harem of three dozen wives, concubines and slaves could not draw their corpulent master from the mattress that served as bed and throne.

A week after Big Turban died of a stroke in 1962, a coup forced the last Imam, his whisky-loving son Muhammad al-Badr, into exile. Few of his subjects, journalist Victoria Clark has written , mourned his end. There were no Yemeni doctors, universities or factories. The Imamate had just one asphalt road, built as a gift from the People’s Republic of China.

Faced with an Arab-nationalist regime linked to Gamal Abdel Nasser’s Egypt, Saudi Arabia financed royalist militias. The governments of Harold Macmillan and Alec Douglas-Home despatched mercenaries for sabotage and gun-running. France, Israel and America followed. The civil war was savage: the Egyptian Air Force attacked civilians in retaliation for assaults on its forces, sometimes using poison gas.

Egypt’s defeat in the Arab-Israeli war of 1967 led Nasser to withdraw from Yemen—and to Saudi Arabia becoming the principal patron of North Yemen’s political class. Elevated to lead North Yemen in 1978, after President Ahmad al-Ghashmi’s assassination, Ali Abdullah Saleh was typical of the political entrepreneurs. Little-educated and from a poor Zaydi peasant family, he purchased influence through control of Army liquor-smuggling rackets.

Ferocious fighting broke out in the British-ruled south as well. The East India Company seized Aden in 1839, claiming it was avenging the looting and rape of Hajj pilgrims from Kochi. After the Suez Canal opened in 1869, Aden became a critical base on the route to India. Britain sought a federation between Aden and surrounding emirates. Left-wing insurgents compelled Harold Wilson’s government to wind down its base and promise to withdraw by 1968.

The only socialist state in the Arab world fought an ever more brutal war with itself, each faction seeking absolute power.

Also read: Explainer-Who are the Houthis, Iran’s allies in Yemen?

Killing time To run Yemen, President Saleh knew he needed Saudi Arabia’s support. Saudi funding of clan chieftains was critical to the political order, enabling Saleh to become patron of the powerful Hashid federation into which he had been born. Its chief, Abdullah al-Ahmar, later explained it thus : “Saleh is my President, but I’m his sheikh.” Three crises then exploded across the Arab world: the revolution in Iran, an Islamist effort to seize Mecca and the emerging jihad in Afghanistan.

From the early 1980s, the Saudis secured their southern flank by despatching neo-fundamentalist proselytisers into the Zaydi highlands. Salafist leader Sheikh Muqbil bin Hadi al-Wadi’i—himself of Zaydi origin—was an unembarrassed anti-Shi’a chauvinist, yet found support. For poorer Zaydis, such as Saleh, the real threat came from élite Sayyid families who had upheld the Imamate. Yemen’s Zaydi Shi’a and Shafe’i Sunnis pray in each other’s mosques and have few ritual markers of difference.

“Local converts from low-status families attracted by the anti-Sayyid thrust of the movement and Sunni Muslims from across the world,” the journalist Ginny Hill has recorded . “Volunteers formed a school militia to patrol the borders and protect the madrassa from their Zaydi neighbours.”

A second strain came from jihadists who had travelled to Afghanistan and fought with al-Qaeda. From 1988, large numbers of Yemeni jihadists returned home, some settling in camps north of Zinjibar. Brigadier Ali Muhsin al-Ahmar, Saleh’s relative and ally, was given charge of organising them into a fighting force. Bin Laden himself is reported to have delivered sermons, asking his men to prepare to liberate Saudi Arabia.

The collapse of the Soviet Union compelled the southern Marxists to ally with the north in 1990, but the alliance soon unravelled. With his new jihadist allies, Saleh gleefully went to war against the so-called infidel leadership in 1994. Leaders like the jihadist commander Tariq al-Fadhli led militia which bulldozed the shrines of saints. The militia of the Muslim Brotherhood-linked Islah party was reported to have attacked churches and vandalised a liquor warehouse holding $7 million in stock.

A reborn Imamate? Less than a decade after becoming ruler of all Yemen, President Saleh’s power began to crumble. Leaders from Aden—often better educated than their counterparts elsewhere—began calling for independence. The events of 9/11 pushed Yemen’s government into a long conflict with al-Qaeda. The Houthis began their march to becoming the principal challenger to Yemen’s rotten state. Fear that Ansar Allah would entrench itself as an Iranian proxy led the Saudi monarchy to war in 2009. That war ended in stalemate; the Arab Spring of 2011 swept Saleh from power. Three years later, Ansar Allah took Sana’a; it would later execute Saleh and fight Saudi Arabia to a stalemate.

There are two paths forward. Like the Arab nationalists of the north, the Communists of the south and the Imamate before them, Ansar Allah could seize all Yemen—and then implode. Alternatively, it could reconcile itself to sharing sovereignty with other actors. Likely, Ansar Allah hopes its actions will yield recognition of its sovereignty through access to central revenues. That, however, would require America and regional powers like Saudi Arabia to accept that the pursuit of hegemony is a dangerous delusion.

Praveen Swami is Contributing Editor at ThePrint. His X handle is @praveenswami. Views are personal.

(Edited by Prashant Dixit)

‘Bereft of logic’: Delhi HC’s earful to ITAT over orders, handling of Patanjali income tax appeals

The court set aside all 7 orders and restored the matters for fresh consideration before a different ITAT bench, making clear that it had not expressed opinion on merits of the tax dispute.

Aditya Edara

16 September, 2026 10:51 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Representational image | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: The Delhi High Court has quashed all seven orders passed by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) in tax appeals involving Patanjali Ayurved Limited, flagging what it called a “shocking picture” of procedural lapses and expressing strong displeasure over the manner in which the tribunal handled the cases.

A bench of Justices Dinesh Mehta and Rajneesh Kumar Gupta said the ITAT order reflected “non-application of mind” and “undue haste”, besides being “bereft of any logic, reasoning or rationale”. The court also referred to a “procedural lacuna” and said the tribunal members had shown “undue haste rather recklessness” in passing and signing the order.

The appeals before the high court were filed by the income tax department, with Patanjali as the respondent. The revenue department challenged the ITAT orders that had earlier granted relief to Patanjali in four appeals.

Show Full Article

The high court set aside all seven orders and restored the matters for fresh consideration before a different ITAT bench, while making clear that it had not expressed any opinion on the merits of the tax dispute.

Four appeals heard, pronounced in a day The procedural issue arose from the manner in which the seven appeals were disposed of by the tribunal. Four appeals filed by Patanjali ITA 534 to 537/Del/2025 concerning assessment years 2013-14 to 2015-16 and 2017-18, were heard and pronounced on 6 August 2025.

Three cross-appeals filed by the revenue department ITA 605 to 607/Del/2025 showed 13 August 2025 as both the date of hearing and date of pronouncement.

Despite the different dates, a common order was passed on 13 August on the cross-appeals filed by the opposites sides. The high court asked how one order could cover appeals heard and pronounced a week apart. The court also noted that the ITAT order contained fewer than seven paragraphs. It clarified that the brevity was not the issue, but the lack of reasoning and application of mind was.

Also Read: Patanjali told to recall 4 tonnes of red chilli powder from market, but no public alert by FSSAI

Assessments challenged before ITAT The seven appeals arose from a search action conducted between 31 October and 3 November 2018, which led to proceedings under Section 153C of the Income Tax Act.

Section 153C enables the tax authorities to assess a person other than the person searched where material found during the search is considered relevant to that person.

The proceedings ultimately culminated in assessment orders dated 27 March 2023. These were subsequently challenged before the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), whose orders passed in November and December 2024 were then taken before the ITAT. The ITAT quashed the four assessments challenged by Patanjali and dismissed the three cross appeals.

ITAT finding challenged  The income tax department then approached the high court against the ITAT orders.

The judgement records that the revenue department’s senior standing counsel Puneet Rai contended that the ITAT had treated the assessment years as “unabated” after the assessing officer issued the Section 153C notice on 6 August 2021, while rejecting the revenue department’s contention on the issue.

The judgement did not decide the appeal on merits. Instead, the high court focused on the procedural defects in the ITAT order. It said the order was “bereft of any logic, reasoning or rationale” and criticised the tribunal members for showing “undue haste rather recklessness” while passing and signing it.

All seven orders set aside The high court said it had “no other option” but to set aside all seven ITAT orders and restore the appeals to their original numbers for fresh adjudication.

The matters will be heard by a different ITAT bench. The court also directed that a copy of its order be sent to the ITAT president and the secretary of the law and justice ministry.

The court clarified that it had made no observation on the merits of the tax dispute. The fresh ITAT bench will therefore be free to examine the issues and take an independent view.

Aditya is an alum of ThePrint School of Journalism, interning with ThePrint.

(Edited by Nardeep Singh Dahiya)

US just accelerated space arms race. What Air Force Secy said about ‘on-orbit space control weapons’

In a move that could accelerate an arms race with Russia and China in Earth’s orbit, the US has confirmed, for the first time, that it has deployed weapons in space.

Ashwin Shekhar

16 September, 2026 06:30 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

File photo of US Space Force Guardians assigned to Space Delta 5 monitor computer workstations at Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, on 18 December, 2025 | David Dozoretz/US Space Forces | Handout via Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: The US has deployed satellites with strike capabilities in Earth’s orbit, Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink said on Monday, in the first such public acknowledgment by the US military.

Speaking at the 2026 Air and Space Cyber Conference in Maryland, Meink said, “We are increasing readiness against existing threats, and the United States has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action.” Meink did not disclose the type of weapons involved or when they were deployed.

The revelation comes amid growing tensions in space involving Russia and China, as the two major military powers increasingly develop capabilities to operate and potentially fight in space.

Show Full Article

Space has also become more critical to modern warfare. Battlefield AI and military infrastructure rely heavily on Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) data, making space an increasingly important domain for strategic defence.

The US and India have traditionally demonstrated anti-satellite (ASAT) capabilities through ground-launched missiles. In March 2019, India’s Mission Shakti used a modified Prithvi Defence Vehicle Mark-2 (PDV MK2) interceptor to destroy the defunct Microsat-E satellite in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). The test was conducted from the APJ Abdul Kalam Island in Odisha.

On the other hand, Russia reportedly operates manoeuvrable “stalker” satellites, including Cosmos 2558, which has been capable of shadowing critical targets such as the commercial ICEYE-X36 satellite supporting Ukrainian intelligence.

China has also expanded its military space capabilities. Its Shijian-21 (SJ-21) satellite is equipped with robotic arms that can physically manoeuvre other satellites into so-called graveyard orbits, where they are effectively removed from operational use.

The militarisation of space dates back to the 1950s, when the US and Soviet Union began competing to develop capabilities to destroy satellites. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty subsequently prohibited the placement of weapons of mass destruction in orbit.

The treaty, however, does not amount to a blanket ban on military activity in space. Russia drew international criticism after destroying one of its defunct satellites in orbit during a ground-based ASAT missile test, creating a large amount of orbital debris.

China criticised the latest US disclosure, with its foreign ministry accusing Washington of “preparing for war in outer space” and warning against turning space “into a battlefield, as well as an arms race there”.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov also reacted to the development and called for “the complete demilitarisation of space”.

Ashwin Shekhar is an alum of ThePrint School of Journalism, currently interning with ThePrint.

(Edited by Chingkheinganbi Mayengbam)
